B

Assess viral replication (quantitative hepatitis B virus [HBV] DNA level) in symptomatic patients with elevated ALT or AST, and in all patients who are carriers of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). B
Offer testing for HIV disease and hepatitis C to all hepatitis B carriers, and vaccinate all patients with chronic HBV against hepatitis A. B
Treatment for acute HBV infection is primarily supportive and does not generally require antiviral therapy. B

Individuals with chronic HBV infection should be treated if they have ALT 2x greater than upper limit of normal (ULN) and elevated HBV-DNA, or if ALT is between ULN and 2x ULN and there is evidence of significant fibrosis (≥F2 or ≥A3). Recommended first-line antiviral drugs include pegylated α-interferon, entecavir, and tenofovir.C

background.definition: Hepatitis B is an infection of the liver caused by HBV. It is a notifiable disease.

list.listitem: In 2006, the overall incidence of hepatitis B in the United States was 1.6 cases per 100,000 per year.
The incidence of hepatitis B in children and adolescents was 0.34 cases per 100,000 per year in 2002.
The prevalence of chronic hepatitis B infection was 0.42% in the United States between 1988 and 1994.
The prevalence of current or past exposure in the United States during that time was 4.9%.
Overall, approximately 1.2 million Americans have chronic hepatitis B infection.
The world-wide prevalence is greatest in nonindustrialized countries.
The costs associated with hepatitis B infection depend on disease severity and are mostly attributed to patients with chronic infection.

The approximate annual cost of caring for a patient with uncomplicated chronic hepatitis B infection is $800, with decompensated hepatic cirrhosis $11,500, liver transplant $86,500, and hepatocellular cancer $7500.
About 2 billion people worldwide have been infected with hepatitis B and more than 350 million have chronic liver infection.
Hepatitis B is caused by HBV, which is a hepadnavirus with eight different genotypes.
HBeAg is more infectious than HBsAg.
Transmission of HBV occurs by percutaneous (bite or needlestick) or mucosal exposure to the blood or body fluids of an infected person or through perinatal transmission from mother to infant.
Transmission of HBV also can occur in settings involving nonsexual interpersonal contact for an extended period (eg, among household contacts of a person with chronic HBV infection).
The incubation period from exposure to clinical hepatitis or serologic evidence of infection is from 1 to 4 months.
Patients exposed to HBV can experience up to four phases of infection (summarized in ): asymptomatic infection, acute inflammatory response, chronic infection/carrier state, or resolution.
Those persons who become chronically infected are sources of transmission of HBV to others.

In patients with chronic HBV infection who develop chronic hepatic inflammation, HBV-infected hepatocytes are destroyed, releasing aminotransferases. Over time, this process leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis.
Among patients with chronic inflammation, the rapid cell destruction and regeneration may lead to spontaneous chromosomal anomalies thought to be responsible for causing hepatocellular carcinoma.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Men who have sex with men (MSM)
Sexual contact with person known to carry hepatitis B
Household contact with person carrying the virus
Residents, immigrants, and children of immigrants in endemic areas

list.listitem: Screen all pregnant women for hepatitis B during their first prenatal visit, A and screen adolescents and adults at high risk for HBV infection, including those born in a high-prevalence country, HIV-positive persons, persons who inject drugs (PWID), household contacts of persons with HBV infection, and men who have sex with men (MSM).B
Vaccination against hepatitis B is recommended for all children younger than 18 years and any adults at risk for hepatitis B infection. B
Vaccinate all patients with chronic HBV against hepatitis A. Offer testing for HIV disease and hepatitis C to all hepatitis B carriers. B
Pregnant persons with hepatitis B should be treated with tenofovir starting at week 28 and their infants should receive both hepatitis B vaccination and HBIG within 12 hours of birth.A

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) and the American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) recommend screening all pregnant women for HBV during their first prenatal visit. It also recommends screening persons at high risk for HBV infection, including those born in a high-prevalence country, HIV-positive persons, injection drug users, household contacts of persons with HBV infection, and men who have sex with men.
Screening should include HBsAg, anti-HBs, and total anti-HBc.

High or intermediate risk regions (>2% seroprevalence) include Africa; north, southeast, and east Asia; Middle east except Cyprus and Israel; Eastern Europe other than Hungary; Malta, Spain and indigenous populations in Greenland; first peoples and Alaskan natives of Alaska and northern Canada; Guatemala and Honduras; Ecuador, Guyana, Suriname, Venezuela, and the Amazon region; and several Caribbean countries including Haiti, Jamaica, Antigua-Barbuda, and Turks and Caicos.

Consider screening for HBV infection in persons born in hyperendemic areas, men who have sex with men, persons who have ever injected drugs, hemodialysis patients, patients infected with the human immunodeficiency virus, and family members, household members, and sexual contacts of HBV-infected persons.
Offer testing for HIV disease and hepatitis C to all hepatitis B carriers because of a high rate of coinfection and shared risk factors.

Give the HBV vaccine to all children younger than 18 years not previously vaccinated. More than 90% of U.S.-born 16- to 19-year-olds who received the HBV vaccine series in infancy demonstrated a seroprotective response to a challenge dose of vaccine.

The HBV vaccine is also recommended for adults at risk for HBV infection. This includes healthcare workers, international travelers to regions with a 2% or higher prevalence of hepatitis B (Africa, East Asia, Eastern Europe, South Pacific, and the Middle East), injection drug users, household contacts of HBsAg-positive persons, men who have sex with men, persons with chronic liver disease, and persons with chronic HIV infection.
Intensified vaccination schedules may be necessary for cirrhotic patients and achieves a better antibody response.
Healthcare workers and others likely to be exposed to potentially infected bodily fluids, such as emergency responders, should use universal precautions to reduce the risk of becoming infected.
Vaccinate all patients with chronic hepatitis B against hepatitis A.

Persons living with HIV may not respond to usual vaccines. A trial randomized 561 persons on antiretroviral therapy with a CD4 count >= 100 cells/mcl to 2 or 3 doses of a novel cytosine phosphoguanine adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine or the standard hepatitis B vaccine. A seroprotective response was seen in 93% receiving 2 doses of the new vaccine, 99.4% receiving 3 doses, and 80.6% receiving the standard vaccine.

American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) guidelines, updated in 2023, recommend universal screening for hepatitis B and C in pregnancy, and vaccination for hepatitis A, B or both based on standard risk factors. Patients who have not previously been screened in adulthood should undergo the triple panel which consists of HBsAg, anti-HBs, and total anti-HBc.

For women with hepatitis (HBsAg positive), quantitiative viral DNA should be measured. Patients with viral load > 200,000 IU/ml should be treated with antivirals. Cesarean section should be based on usual obstetric indications and not on the presence of infection. Neonates of persons who are HBsAg positive or who have unknown status should receive both hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth.

A trial randomized 280 pregnant persons to: 1) tenofovir fumarate started at week 16 + HBV vaccination for infants or 2) standard care in China which is tenofovir fumarate started at week 28 + HBV vaccination and HBIG for infants. The new regimen was non-inferior both in intention to treat analysis (0.76% vs 0.0% transmission) and per protocol analysis (0.0% vs 0.0%). There was a trend toward more congenital malformations in the standard care group (6.3% vs 2.3%, 95% CI -8.8% to 0.7%).
Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and hepatitis B vaccine to sexual partners of patients with acute HBV infection.

Give hepatitis B vaccination and HBIG (200 IU IM) to infants born to mothers with chronic hepatitis B. Without these measures, about 88% of these infants will acquire chronic HBV infection, compared with 6% of those receiving it (NNT = 2).
Give HBIG and the HBV vaccination series to unvaccinated persons with a significant exposure to fluids contaminated with HBsAg.
Give the HBV vaccination series to unvaccinated persons with a significant exposure to fluids and whose HBsAg status is unknown.
Give a booster dose of the HBV vaccine to previously vaccinated persons without a postvaccination proof of immunity who subsequently have a significant exposure to fluids contaminated with HBsAg.
Postexposure prophylaxis in not needed in previously vaccinated persons who have a significant exposure to fluids of unknown HBsAg status, even those without postvaccination proof of immunity.

In patients with HBV infection who are either surface antigen positive or core antigen positive, antiviral prophylaxis is recommended by American Gastroenterology Association (AGA) guidelines (2025) for moderate to high risk patients requiring immunosuppressive therapy. Patients at low risk should be monitored without antiviral prophylaxis. Individuals at risk for reactivation should be screened using triple-panel testing with HBV surface antigen, hepatitis B surface antibody, and total hepatitis B core antibody.
Chronic hepatitis B is defined as the presence of HBsAg for 6 or more months. C
Assess viral replication (quantitative HBV DNA level) in symptomatic patients with elevated ALT or AST, and in all patients who are carriers of HBsAg. B

Liver biopsy is recommended in patients with active disease as manifested by an elevated ALT or AST, persistent presence of HBeAg, more than 100,000 copies/mL HBV DNA, if treatment is being considered and when other conditions exist such as alcoholism or coinfection with hepatitis C or HIV. B

Measurement of liver elasticity does not predict the likelihood of clinically significant portal hypertension in patients with hepatitis B (it is more useful in hepatitis C and alcohol related liver disease. B

list.listitem: summarizes the diagnostic criteria for hepatitis B infection, including chronic infection, inactive carrier state, and resolved infection.
Suspect acute hepatitis B infection in the patient with risk factors for HBV who complains of fatigue, malaise, upper abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and fever.
Most patients acutely infected with HBV have no symptoms, whereas one-third to one-half of children older than 5 years and adults develop symptoms.

Uncommon signs and symptoms include extrahepatic symptoms such as rash, arthritis, and polyarteritis nodosa. Arthralgias occur in 10% to 20% of patients with acute hepatitis B. Jaundice appears later in the course of the disease and can occur in as many as three-fourths of patients.
Patients with chronic HBV infection typically have no symptoms unless they develop chronic liver disease.
Patients with acute fulminant hepatitis present with deep jaundice, cerebral symptoms, and progressive liver damage.

In acute HBV infection, serum aminotransferases (AST/ALT) are typically 500 to 10,000 IU/L. In chronic HBV infection, serum aminotransferase levels are normal or minimally elevated (<100 IU/L). Only in severe late-stage disease are serum aminotransferase levels elevated.

Elevated ALT, AST, and GGT modestly increase the likelihood of hepatitis B when used as a screening tool in men; elevation in patients with known hepatitis B suggests active disease. An elevated AST or ALT is modestly useful in identifying patients with biopsy-proven chronic active hepatitis.
While serology confirms the diagnosis of HBV infection, it is more helpful in determining the stage of infection. summarizes how to interpret HBV serology.

Chronic hepatitis B infection is defined as the presence of HBsAg for 6 or more months. Evaluation of patients with chronic hepatitis B should include quanitification HPV-DNA levels. Levels of HBV-DNA less than 2000 IU/ml suggest inactive infection, and levels greater than 20,000 IU/ml suggest active disease.

HBeAg, antibody to HBeAg (anti-HBe), and HBV DNA are markers of active virus replication and infectivity and should be assessed in patients with chronic HBV, as they help guide treatment in combination with ALT levels.
CT of the abdomen is the recommended initial imaging study for patients with jaundice and either acute abdominal pain and fever or who are asymptomatic but have chronic symptoms.

In patients with chronic hepatitis B, the ratio of red blood cell distribution width (%) to platelet count (10^9L) is an indicator of fibrosis, with increasing levels indicating greater risk. A cutoff of >0.17 had LR+ 6.2 and LR- 0.46 (sensitivity 58%, specificity 96%).
Another predictor of cirrhosis in hepatitis B is the red cell distribution width to lymphocyte ratio, with 88% sensitivity and 72% specificity at a cutoff of 10.87.
Distinguish acute infection from chronic infection based on the presence of symptoms and the duration of laboratory abnormalities.
Evaluate all patients with chronic HBV for signs of chronic liver disease as well as coinfection with hepatitis C, HIV, and hepatitis delta.
summarizes the indications for liver biopsy.
Acute hepatitis B infection does not require antiviral therapy. B
Individuals with chronic HBV infection, either positive or negative for HBeAg, with elevated aminotransferases and HBV DNA greater than 20,000 copies/mL are candidates for antiviral therapy. B

While treatment can begin with any of the drugs approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases 2018 guidelines recommend pegylated α-interferon, entecavir, or tenofovir as first-line treatment.C
Patients with chronic HBV infection who do not have HBeAg need to be treated for longer durations, at least 1 year. B
The primary treatment for acute hepatitis B infection is supportive.

A Cochrane review found no evidence of benefit for any intervention for acute HBV infection, based on very low quality of evidence. Lamivudine, compared to placebo, no intervention or entecavir, may even result to higher rates of chronic HBV infection, based on low to very low quality evidence. Interferon may increase adverse events, based on low quality evidence.

Treatment with antiviral medications (eg, tenofovir or entecavir) is indicated for patients with fulminant hepatitis B and those with protracted, severe acute hepatitis B. However, clinical trials are lacking.

For patients without cirrhosis who are HBsAg and HBeAg positive, treatment is indicated if their ALT is 2x the upper limit of normal (ULN, 35 U/L in men and 25 U/L in women) and the HBV-DNA is >20,000 IU/ml. If the ALT is between ULN and 2x ULN and HBV-DNA is >20,000 IU/ml, treat if liver bioipsy or non-invasive testing finds ≥F2 or ≥A3 fibrosis.

While treatment can begin with any of the drugs approved by the FDA, the 2018 guidelines from American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases recommends pegylated α-interferon-2a 180 mcg weekly (adults), pegylated α-interferon-2b (children), tenofovir dipovaxil fumarate 300 mg daily, tenofovir alafenamide 25 mg daily, or entecavir 0.5 mg daily as first-line treatment. Lamivudine, adefovir, and telbivudine are classified by the guideline as non-preferred treatments.

The 2018 AASLD guidelines found that for patients who are HBeAg positive, HBV-DNA suppression was achieved most often in those taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (76%) or tenofovir alafenamide (73%). For those who are HBeAg negative, cure rates were highest for entecavir (90%-91%), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (93%) or tenofovir alafenamide (90%).

For patients without cirrhosis who are HBsAg positive and HBeAg negative, treatment is recommended when ALT is 2x ULN and HBV-DNA is >2000 IU/ml. If the ALT is between ULN and 2x ULN and HBV-DNA is >2,000 IU/ml, treat if liver bioipsy or non-invasive testing finds ≥F2 or ≥A3 fibrosis.

For patients without cirrhosis who are HBsAg positive, treatment is not recommended if ALT is less than ULN and HBV_DNA is <2000 IU/ml for HBeAg negative patients and <20,000 IU/ml for HBeAg positive patients.

Bulevirtide is a peptidic entry inhibitor for treatment of hepatitis D and B coinfection. In a phase 2 trial, adults with chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis D coinfection were randomized to placebo or bulevirtide 2 mg, 5 mg or 10 mg for 24 weeks. Among those receiving active drug 50% to 77% achieved undetectable levels of hepatitis D, but by week 48 viral levels had recurred. Serious adverse events occurred in 4% to 9% of treated patients.

Xalnesiran is an RNA interfering molecule that inhibits replication. A study randomized 159 participants with to 5 groups differing by xalnesiran dose and whether it was paired with pegylated interferon alfa-2a or ruzotolimod. All participants had chronic hepatitis B and had received a nucleotide analogue (entecavir, tenofovir alafenamide, or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) for at least 12 months. The best results were seen in the group receiving xalnesiran + peg interferon alfa-2a with 20% having undetectable HBsAg after 24 weeks. However, this group also had the most adverse events, most commonly elevation in alanine aminotransferase. This was a phase 2 trial and further study is needed.

A trial randomized patients with chronic hepatitis D to peginterferon alfa-2a monotherapy, bulevirtide monotherapy, or combination therapy for 48 weeks. They found that 24 weeks after the end of treatment, undetectable levels of hepatitis D RNA was more likely with combination therapy than in the monotherapy groups (46% for combination, 25% for peginterferon only, and 12% with bulevirtide alone).

A randomized trial comparing entecavir with tenofovir found no difference in levels of DNA suppression or side effects at 144 weeks. There was also no difference in the likelihood of clinical progression or complications.

A non-inferiority trial randomized 1002 patients with chronic hepatitis B to tenofovir amibufenamide (TMF) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF, the standard therapy). TMF was non-inferior at achieving HBV DNA <20 IU/ml both for patients who were HBeAg positive (50.2% vs 53.7%) and for those who were HBeAg negative (88.9% vs 87.8%). TMF was as well tolerated with less adverse effects on bone density and serum creatinine than TDF.

An RCT randomized 160 persons with chronic hepatitis B infection and ALT between 1x and 2x the upper limit of normal to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 mg or placebo once daily for 3 years. At the end of tha ttime, fewer patients in the tenofovir group had progression in their fibrosis (26% vs 47%, p < 0.05, NNT = 5). Treatment had no impact on progression of necroinflammation (7% vs 16%, p = 0.08).

A Canadian study with 67 patients who had been treated with a nucleoside analogue for at least one year and had undetectable HBV DNA and hepaitis B e-antigen seroconversion, the medication was discontinued in 45 patients. After 72 weeks, 15 of 45 had virological or biochemical relapse, and 17 of 45 were retreated.

A multicenter, international study of 475 patients (82% Asians, 55% treated with entecavir) concluded that serum levels of HBsAg <100 IU/mL and HBV DNA <100 IU/mL 24 weeks off-treatment are good predictors of low relapse risk and HBsAg loss. The authors suggested that these two parameters can be used as early surrogate endpoints in trials evaluating finite therapy for HBV.

A Phase 2 trial evaluated bepirovirsen (an antisense oligonucleotide targetting mRNA) in patients with chronic HPV infection. The drug resulted in sustaned HBsAg and HBV DNA loss in about 10% of participants. Larger and longer trials are needed to confirm these findings. Safety was adequate.
Pretreatment with corticosteroids before starting α-interferon results in speedier clearance of HbeAg and HBV DNA, but the effect on clinical outcomes is not known.
Using bile acids improves normalization of aminotransferase levels but is no better than placebo in viral clearance, and the effect on clinical outcomes is not known.

Indications for liver transplantation include acute liver failure, end-stage liver disease, cirrhosis accompanied by major complications (eg, ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy), patients who develop the hepatorenal syndrome, and children who deviate from their growth curve.
While the quality of research on milk thistle (Silybum marianum) in chronic hepatitis is poor, it appears to be no better than placebo in decreasing death, disease progression, or complications.

A number of studies have evaluated bicyclol, herbal medicine (eg, Radix Sophorae flavescentis, phyllanthus species), traditional Chinese medicine (eg, Xiao Chai Hu Tang), and acupuncture in treating asymptomatic HBV carriers and patients with chronic HBV infection. In general, the benefit is at best comparable to placebo, the quality of the studies is generally poor, and the evidence is mostly uncertain.
There is insufficient evidence for vitamin D supplementation for improving outcomes for adults with chronic liver diseases (including chronic HBV), based on a Cochrane review of 27 RCTs.
Patients with hepatitis B infection should refrain from alcohol use and the use of medications that may be hepatotoxic.
Patients should consume foods rich in calories and carbohydrates during the acute stages of the disease.
Patients positive for HBeAg should be treated with interferon for 16 weeks, while those not carrying HBeAg should receive interferon for one year.

Patients positive for HBeAg should be treated with lamivudine for one year, while those not carrying HBeAg should receive lamivudine for at least one year, although the optimal duration of treatment is unknown.
Patients with acute fulminant hepatitis may require intensive care and should also be referred for possible liver transplantation.
Patients with chronic hepatitis B should undergo periodic surveillance to detect early hepatocellular carcinoma.C
However, there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the value of screening patients with hepatitis B with alpha-fetoprotein or ultrasound to detect early liver carcinoma.C
Healthcare workers experiencing needlestick injuries are at the greatest risk of infection if the source contains HBeAg. B
Coinfection with hepatitis D is associated with a more severe infection and much worse prognosis. B
85% to 95% recover spontaneously from acute hepatitis B infection.
There is significant geographic variation in long-term outcomes of chronic HBV.

The rate of hepatocellular carcinoma in men from Taiwan without HBsAg or HBeAg was 39 per 100,000 person-years. In men positive for only HBsAg, it was 324 per 100,000 person-years, and for men positive for both HBsAg and HBeAg, it was 1169 per 100,000 person-years.

In a study of patients under age 40 with chronic hepatitis B infection, the incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma was low (2.5/1000 person-years). It was highest among those with FIB-4 < 0.70 (0.17/1000 person-years) and highest in those with radiologic evidence of cirrhosis (31/1000 person-years).

After 30 years of follow-up of Italian volunteers for blood donation found to have HBsAg, the rates of clinically significant liver disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, and other liver-related complications were similar to those of uninfected control patients.

In healthcare workers sustaining needlestick injuries from needles contaminated with HBV, 22% to 31% develop clinical hepatitis, and 37% to 62% develop serologic evidence of HBV infection if the blood contained both HBsAg and HBeAg, compared with 1% to 6% and 23% to 37%, respectively, when the infected blood contains no HBeAg.
See for monitoring recommendations.
An observational supported regular monitoring for hepatocellular carcinoma in patients with Child-Pugh class A or B cirrhosis caused by hepatitis B.
Mothers who carry HBsAg may breastfeed.
Vaccinate sexual and household contacts against HBV.
Until their sexual partners' immunity is established, patients with hepatitis B should use barrier protection during sexual intercourse.
Advise patients not to share toothbrushes or razors.
Patients may participate in all activities, including contact sports, daycare, etc.
It is acceptable to share food and utensils and to kiss others.

American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) guidelines, updated in 2023, recommend universal screening for hepatitis B and C in pregnancy at an early prenatal visit, and vaccination for hepatitis A, B or both based on standard risk factors. Patients who have not previously been screened in adulthood should undergo the triple panel which consists of HBsAg, anti-HBs, and total anti-HBc.

For women with hepatitis (HBsAg positive), quantitiative viral DNA should be measured. Patients with viral load > 200,000 IU/ml should be treated with antivirals. Cesarean section should be based on usual obstetric indications and not on the presence of infection. Neonates of persons who are HBsAg positive or who have unknown status should receive both hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth.

The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine guidelines (2025) recommend triple-panel testing (hepatis B surface antigen, antibody to hepatis B surface antigen, and total antibody to hepatitis B core antigen) at the initial prenatal visit. For women with a previous documented triple panel negative test, only hepatitis B surface antigen screening is needed. All unvaccinated women without serologic evidence of immunity should receive hepatitis B vaccination during pregnancy.

The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine guidelines also recommend that women with > 200,000 U/ml receive antiretroviral therapy with tenofovir in the 3rd trimester, beginning at 28 to 32 weeks gestation. Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) should be given to all infants of mothers who are hepatitis B surface antigen positive within 12 hours of birth, whether or not tenofovir was given during pregnancy.

Compared with untreated controls, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG; 200 IU) given intravenously every 4 weeks starting at 28 weeks of gestation reduced the rate of HBeAg positivity from 79% to 21% (NNT = 2).
A systematic review of 16 RCTs with 2440 HBsAg positive pregnant women found that both HBIG and vaccination reduced the likelihood that their newborns would be infected.

A systematic review identified 19 studies with 1092 mothers of tenofovir, 40 studies with 2080 mothers of lamivudine, and 83 studies with 6036 mothers of telbivudine. All three were highly effective at preventing mother to child transmission (odds ratio 0.1 for tenofovir, 0.16 for lamivudine, and 0.14 for telbivudine). Antiviral therapy should be considered for women with high HBV DNA levels (> 200,000 IU/ml) or who are positive for HBeAg.

A trial randomized 280 pregnant persons to: 1) tenofovir fumarate started at week 16 + HBV vaccination for infants or 2) standard care in China which is tenofovir fumarate started at week 28 + HBV vaccination and HBIG for infants. The new regimen was non-inferior both in intention to treat analysis (0.76% vs 0.0% transmission) and per protocol analysis (0.0% vs 0.0%). There was a trend toward more congenital malformations in the standard care group (6.3% vs 2.3%, 95% CI -8.8% to 0.7%).

A randomized trial compared tenofovir with placebo in 331 pregnant women who were hepatitis B e antigen positive. The rate of transmissions was 3 of 147 in the placebo group and 0 of 14 in the tenofovir group, but this difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.12).

A Cochrane review evaluating the role of antivirals for the prevention of HBV mother-to-child transmission among HIV-coinfected pregnant women found uncertain evidence for the efficacy and safety of tenofovir-based antiviral combination regimens.
Management of chronic HBV in children is similar to that for adults.
See screening and prevention section for postexposure prophylaxis against maternal transmission.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Hepatitis B Infection.
feature.feature_body:
Chronic Hepatitis B Inactive HBsAg Carrier State Resolved Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) Present at least 6 mo Present at least 6 mo Negative
Serum hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA >20,000 IU/mL (10,000 copies/mL) <2000 IU/mL (1000 copies/mL) Undetectable (very low levels may be detected using sensitive PCR assays)
ALT/AST levels Persistent or intermittent elevation Persistently normal Normal
Liver biopsy Chronic hepatitis with moderate or severe necroinflammation Absence of significant hepatitis
Data from Lok AS, McMahon BJ. Corrections to AASLD guidelines on chronic hepatitis B. Hepatology 2007;45(6):1347.

feature.caption: Indications for Liver Biopsy in Patients Chronically Infected with Hepatitis B.
feature.feature_body: Persistent elevation of ALT (>twice upper limit of normal for 3-6 mo) Persistent presence of hepatitis B early antigen (HBeAg) More than 100,000 copies/mL of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA Patient is being considered for treatment Other conditions may be present (eg, hepatitis C infection, alcoholism, etc.) Data from Lok AS, McMahon BJ. Corrections to AASLD guidelines on chronic hepatitis B. Hepatology 2007;45(6):1347.

feature.caption: Interpretation of Hepatitis B Serology.
feature.feature_body:
HBsAg HBsAb HBc-IgG HBc-IgM HBeAg HBeAb
Not infected (susceptible) − − − − − −
Immune due to vaccination − + − − − −
Immune due to natural infection − + + − − +
Acute infection, early phase + − − − Either + or − −
Acute infection, late phase + − + +++ + −
Chronically infected (carrier, high infection risk) + − + Either + or − + −
Chronically infected (carrier, lower infection risk) + − + − − +
Abbreviations: HBsAg, hepatitis B surface antigen; HBSAb, hepatitis B surface antibody; HBc-IgG, hepatitis B core antibody, immunoglobulin G; HBc-IgM, hepatitis B core antibody, immunoglobulin M; HBeAg; hepatitis B early antigen; HBeAb, hepatitis B early antibody. Adapted from Mast EE, Margolis HS, Fiore AE, et al.; Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). A comprehensive immunization strategy to eliminate transmission of hepatitis B virus infection in the United States: recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) part 1: immunization of infants, children, and adolescents. MMWR Recomm Rep 2005;54(RR-16):1-31.

feature.caption: Hepatitis B Stages.
feature.feature_body:
Immune Tolerance Immune Activation/Reactivation Immunological Surveillance Resolution
Clinical Acute infection, incubation period Inflammatory response Carrier state, mostly inactive Immunity, resolved disease
HBsAg Positive Positive Positive Negative
HBV DNA (log IU/mL) High, >7 Decreasing/fluctuating, 7-3.3 Low, <3.3 Undetectable
Liver inflammation None or minimal Mild to severe None or minimal None
ALT Normal Continuous or intermittent elevation Normal Normal
HBeAg Positive Positive or negative Negative Negative
Prognosis Uncertain, favorable for the majority Progressive inflammation and necrosis may cause cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma Favorable for most, but some are at increased risk for hepatocellular carcinoma Good
Transmission High High, decreasing Low None
Abbreviations: HBeAg, hepatitis B early antigen; HBsAg, hepatitis B surface antigen; HBV, hepatitis B virus. Adapted from Lindh M, Uhnoo I, Blackberg J, et al. Treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection: an update of Swedish recommendations. Scand J Infect Dis 2008;40:436-450.
